newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Peregrine warns of risks in Thai zero-coupon bonds.
newsitem.headline: Peregrine warns of risks in Thai zero-coupon bonds.

text.p: Investors contemplating Thailand's bailout bonds should be aware of the greater risks of zero coupon bonds generally as well as the special risks in the Thai bond market, Peregrine Fixed Income said on Wednesday.

"There is a real possibility that Thailand's yield curve will steepen and if it does in such a way that the long end yields move higher, then bailout bonds will be hit the worst," Greg Batey, head of market research at Peregrine, said in a report issued Wednesday.
"The zero will be issued a double whammy -- experiencing the greatest yield increase through the spot (or zero coupon) yield curve, which will be amplified through the bond's long duration," he said.
Thailand will issue 50 billion baht of seven-year zero coupon bonds on Friday.
Proceeds of the issue will be used by the government-run Property Loans Management Organization (PLMO) to purchase non-performing property loans from banks and financial companies.
The government has said the total size of the issue could rise to 100 billion baht, or US$3.85 billion, in future.

Batey said one of the reasons Thailand's yield curve is so flat is that investors tend to buy bonds that generate sufficient cash flow to exceed the investor's cost of funds and that present little risk of default.
Up to now, there has been little sensitivity to a bond's maturity and, therefore, its market risk.
But that is likely to change following an accounting rule change last summer that requires investors to mark to market their assets each month rather than carry them at book value.
"Instead of carrying assets at book value, the value of assets of these financial institutions are now exposed to changes in interest rates," said Batey.

"As a result, holdings of bonds with longer duration show greater variability to any change in interest rates," he said. Because of this, investors will become more sensitive to a bond's maturity and will demand a higher yield to compensate for the greater market risk.
In cases of market volatility, zero coupon bonds are more risky than coupon bonds because of their longer duration.
Also, spot yields increase more than coupon yields of equal maturity when a yield curve steepens, Batey said.

"Unless investors are convinced that interest rates will decline over the near-to-medium term, they need to be compensated for the greater risk the bailout bonds represent compared to coupon bonds," Batey said.
